newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich promises House vote on tax cut this year.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich promises House vote on tax cut this year.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich, re-emphasising tax cuts after appearing to back off them last month, said Wednesday he would put a tax cut to a vote this year with or without President Clinton's blessing.
"We will vote on a tax cut even if President Clinton opposes it. We will give the president a chance to veto a tax cut if he wants to," the Georgia Republican said.
Gingrich last month sparked a furore among some conservative Republicans when he said that a tax cut should perhaps be considered after a balanced budget is worked out.
Those remarks were seen by some Republicans as backing off from a key party goal. Gingrich has since emphasised that he is very committed to tax reduction.
House leaders have not yet said how big a tax cut they want. When Gingrich was asked about that, he said he wanted one "as big as possible."

Clinton in his budget proposed $98 billion in tax cuts and Senate Republicans have said they want about twice that amount. Congressional budget leaders were meeting with White House budget officials this week to try and work out sticky issues.
Republican leaders have said taxes is one area where they want to see some movement from the White House.
Gingrich said he favoured a zero capital gains tax and estate tax.

"We are going to have a tax cut this year, we hope the president will sign it," Gingrich said. "We favour very low taxes, we favour abolishing the tax on savings and job creation, we favour abolishing the tax on death benefits," he added.
A House vote on a tax cut would occur at the latest by October, Gingrich said. The new fiscal year begins Oct. 1.
Meanwhile, a House vote was planned on two tax-related bills for April 15, the tax filing deadline.

One bill would be an amendment to the U.S. Constitution to require a two-thirds vote of Congress to pass a tax increase, except in times of war or national emergency. The amendment itself requires a two-thirds vote of the House and Senate to pass.

The other bill would create criminal penalties for Internal Revenue Service employees who snoop into taxpayer files. The punishment would be a fine of up to $100,000 and/or imprisonment of not more than one year.
The legislation would also require the IRS to notify the victim of unauthorised browsing and allow victims to seek civil penalties.
